title: Intensity in practice
goal: Plan a week for an amateur with limited hours: keep easy days easy, choose the hard work, and say honestly how strong the evidence is.

steps.title: Make easy days really easy
steps.text:
Every distribution that works has one thing in common: most training is zone 1, below LT1. The trial that tested this most directly put 12 subelite runners on 5 months of training with the same zone 3 share (about 8%) but more or less zone 1: **80/12/8** vs **67/25/8**. The group with more zone 1 improved its 10.4 km cross-country time more: **157 s vs 121.5 s** [[c:ip-esteve]]. In an earlier study of 8 runners, more zone 1 time went with faster races [[c:ip-esteve-corr]].

In practice: on easy days you can talk in full sentences (the [talk test](g:talk-test)), with heart rate or power under LT1. 'Steady' rides that creep above it turn zone 1 into zone 2.

claims.text: In 12 subelite runners over 5 months, more zone 1 (80/12/8 vs 67/25/8) gave a larger 10.4 km improvement (157 vs 121.5 s).

evidence.quote: The magnitude of the improvement in running performance was significantly greater (p = 0.03) in Z1 (-157 +/- 13 seconds) than in Z2 (-121.5 +/- 7.1 seconds).

claims.text: In 8 subelite runners, total zone 1 time correlated with faster cross-country race times (r = −0.79 and −0.97).

evidence.quote: A correlation coefficient of r=-0.79 (P=0.06) and r=-0.97 (P=0.008) was found between the total training time spent in zone 1 and performance time during the short and long cross-country races, respectively.

steps.title: Few hours: is more zone 2 fine?
steps.text:
Elite patterns come from athletes training 10 or more times a week. With 4–6 hours, the picture may change. Foster and colleagues (pro-polarised) write that athletes with lower training loads are less likely to be harmed by threshold-centred training [[c:ip-foster-low]]. Burnley and colleagues add that zone 2 work matches the demands of races lasting about 25 min to 3 h; cyclists call its upper part [sweet-spot training](g:sweet-spot-training) [[c:ip-specific]].

In 38 recreational runners over 8 weeks, a zone 2-heavy plan (**40/50/10**) improved as much as a polarised one (**77/3/20**) on 17% less training time [[c:ip-festa]]. In 30 recreational runners, polarised improved 10 km time by 5.0% vs 3.6%, a difference that was not significant [[c:ip-munoz]].

claims.text: Athletes with lower training frequency and load are less likely to experience negative effects from threshold-centred training.

evidence.quote: Less accomplished athletes with lower training frequency/load are less likely to experience negative effects from threshold centric training, although our collective experience still supports the value of an approach to training dominated by a TID favoring low-intensity training.

claims.text: Regular zone 2 training is specific to races in the heavy domain (about 25 min to 3 h); many successful athletes use substantial 'sweet spot' work just below critical power.

evidence.quote: On specificity grounds, regular training in zone 2 will be especially important for athletes whose races emphasize the heavy exercise intensity domain (i.e., competition duration between approximately 25 min and 3 h).
have often incorporated significant quantities of Zone 2 training (colloquially known as “sweet spot” training, just below the critical power/speed) in their programs

claims.text: In 38 recreational runners over 8 weeks, a focused (40/50/10) plan gave similar improvements to a polarised (77/3/20) plan with 17% less training time.

evidence.quote: Focused Endurance Training obtains similar improvements than Polarized Endurance Training saving 17% of training time in recreational runners.

claims.text: In 30 recreational runners over 10 weeks, polarised and between-threshold training improved 10 km time by 5.0% and 3.6%, a non-significant difference.

evidence.quote: Improvements were 5.0% vs 3.6%, ~41 s difference at post-training-intervention. This difference was not significant.

steps.title: Building a week
steps.text:
A workable week for 4–8 hours:

- **One zone 3 session**: for example 5 × 4 min above critical power.
- **One zone 2 session**, if your race lives in the heavy domain: 2 × 20 min sweet spot, or a tempo run.
- **Everything else zone 1**, including one longer session.
- **Hard day, easy day**: never two hard sessions back to back. Reviewers of elite runners recommend exactly this, shifting from pyramidal towards polarised as races approach [[c:ip-hard-easy]].

Count it by time and such a week comes out pyramidal: the warm-ups and recoveries of the hard sessions are zone 1 too.

claims.text: Highly trained and elite runners are encouraged to train on a hard day–easy day basis, shifting from pyramidal to polarised towards competition.

evidence.quote: Highly trained and elite middle- and long-distance runners are encouraged to adopt a traditional periodization pattern with a hard day-easy day basis
consisting in a shift from a pyramidal TID used during the preparatory and precompetitive periods toward a polarized TID during the competitive period

steps.title: Check the plan's distribution
steps.problem: A cyclist with 6 h a week plans: Tue 75 min with 5 × 4 min in zone 3; Thu 75 min with 2 × 20 min sweet spot (zone 2); Sat 150 min easy; Sun 60 min easy. Everything outside the efforts is zone 1. What is the time-in-zone distribution?
steps: Zone 1 > 2 > 3: pyramidal, with five-sixths of the time easy.

steps.title: How sure can we be?
steps.text:
Be honest about the evidence for amateurs. The trials are small (30–42 people), short (8–10 weeks) and all in runners. In each, **every group improved** and the differences between plans were small [[c:ip-all-improve]]. One hint points the other way from the 'go hard' instinct: in 42 recreational runners, more people failed to respond to the high-intensity and polarised blocks than to the low-intensity one [[c:ip-zinner]].

So for a time-crunched amateur: keep easy days easy, include some hard work, and choose between zone 2 and zone 3 for the hard part by race demands and what you'll do consistently. The data don't yet pick one.

claims.text: In recreational trials, all distributions improved performance, with small or no differences between them.

evidence.quote: No differences were found between the groups on any parameter investigated except about the total training time
Both groups significantly improved their 10K time

claims.text: In 42 recreational runners, the risk of not responding was greater with high-intensity and polarised blocks than with low-intensity training.

evidence.quote: Based on the individual response of recreational runners the relative risk of nonresponding is greater with HIGH and POL compared with LOW.

points: All successful distributions are mostly zone 1: easy days should pass the talk test and stay under LT1.
More zone 1 (80/12/8 vs 67/25/8) improved subelite runners more, in one small trial.
With few hours, zone 2-heavy plans did about as well as polarised in small recreational trials, and zone 2 is race-specific for 25 min–3 h events.
A practical week: one zone 3 session, one zone 2 session if your race needs it, the rest easy, hard day–easy day.
Evidence for amateurs is weak: small, short trials where every plan improved.

variants.stem: A triathlete's LT1 heart rate on the bike is 135 bpm. On his 'easy' rides with a club, he averages 148 bpm and can only speak in short phrases. What should he change?

options.text: Ride easier, under 135 bpm, so easy rides are really zone 1
options.why: Right: 148 bpm and short phrases put him above LT1, in zone 2.

options.text: Nothing: 148 bpm is still well below his threshold
options.why: It is below LT2 but above LT1: zone 2, not zone 1.

options.text: Ride even harder, since group rides are good training
options.why: That turns his easy days into a block of zone 2 and adds strain.

options.text: Switch to a fixed 70% HRmax target
options.why: A fixed percentage could still sit above his own LT1.

variants.stem: In 8 runners, zone 1 time correlated r = −0.97 with race time. What is the main limit of this finding?

options.text: A correlation in 8 runners can't show cause
options.why: Right: fitter runners may simply run more easy volume; a tiny observational sample can't show cause.

options.text: r = −0.97 means zone 1 time made them slower
options.why: Negative r with race time means more zone 1 went with faster (shorter) times.

options.text: The correlation is too weak to matter
options.why: −0.97 is very strong; the issue is design and size, not strength.

options.text: Heart-rate zones can't be measured in runners
options.why: Heart-rate zones from a lab test are standard in runners.

variants.stem: In 38 recreational runners, a 40/50/10 plan gave similar gains to a 77/3/20 polarised plan on 17% less time. What does this best support?

options.text: For recreational runners, a zone 2-heavy plan can work as well on less time
options.why: Right: that is what this small 8-week trial found.

options.text: Polarised training doesn't work for recreational runners
options.why: The polarised group improved too, just not more.

options.text: Threshold training is better than polarised for everyone
options.why: Similar gains in one small trial don't show it is better, or for everyone.

options.text: Training time doesn't affect fitness
options.why: The plans were matched for training load, so the less-time plan was simply harder per minute.

variants.stem: A cyclist with 5 h a week targets a 40 km time trial (about 60 min). Which plan fits the evidence best?

options.text: Mostly easy riding plus one sweet-spot and one zone 3 session a week
options.why: Right: easy base, race-specific zone 2, some zone 3; zone 2 suits a heavy-domain race.

options.text: Only zone 1, since elites do 80–90% easy
options.why: With 5 h, all easy riding likely gives too little stimulus; elites also do hard work.

options.text: Only zone 3 intervals, to save time
options.why: Little evidence supports all-high-intensity weeks, and non-response risk was higher with high-intensity blocks.

options.text: Avoid zone 2 completely: it is a 'black hole'
options.why: Both sides of the debate accept zone 2 has a role; for a 60 min race it is specific.

variants.stem: A runner with 4 h a week plans: Tue 50 min with 5 × 3 min in zone 3; Thu 50 min with 20 min tempo in zone 2; Fri 50 min easy; Sun 90 min easy. The rest is zone 1. What share of time is zone 1?

options.text: About 85%
options.why: Right: 205 of 240 min.
That is the session count: 2 of 4 sessions are easy.

options.text: About 58%
options.why: That counts only the two easy runs (140 min) as zone 1.

options.text: About 94%
options.why: Forgets the 20 min tempo: only the 15 min of zone 3 was removed.

variants.stem: A triathlete trains 8 h a week (480 min), with 60 min in zone 2 and 30 min in zone 3; the rest is zone 1. What share is zone 2?

options.why: That is the zone 3 share (30/480).
That adds zones 2 and 3 together (90/480).
That is the zone 1 share (390/480).

variants.stem: A time-crunched cyclist (4 h, 240 min) plans: Tue 60 min with 3 × 12 min sweet spot; Thu 60 min with 2 × 20 min sweet spot; Sat 120 min easy. The rest is zone 1, no zone 3. Which shape is it by time?

options.text: Pyramidal: about 68/32/0
options.why: Right: zone 1 = 164 min (68%), zone 2 = 76 min (32%), zone 3 = 0, so Z1 > Z2 > Z3.

options.text: Threshold: zone 2 is the largest share
options.why: Zone 2 is 32%, zone 1 still 68%.

options.text: Polarised: lots of zone 1, little zone 2
options.why: Polarised needs zone 3 above zone 2; there is no zone 3 at all.

options.text: Pyramidal: about 50/50/0
options.why: That treats the two sweet-spot sessions as all zone 2 (120 of 240 min).

variants.solution: Zone 2 = 36 + 40 = 76 min. Zone 1 = 240 − 76 = 164 min. 164/240 = 68%, 76/240 = 32%, zone 3 = 0. Z1 > Z2 > Z3: pyramidal, with a big zone 2 share and a polarisation index of 0.

variants.stem: A runner has two hard sessions (intervals, tempo) and three easy runs to fit into Mon–Sun with Friday off. Which order follows the hard day–easy day principle?

options.text: Tue intervals, Wed easy, Thu tempo, Sat easy, Sun easy long run
options.why: Right: each hard day is followed by an easy day or rest.

options.text: Tue intervals, Wed tempo, Thu easy, Sat easy, Sun easy long run
options.why: The two hard sessions are back to back.

options.text: Mon easy, Tue easy, Wed easy, Sat intervals, Sun tempo
options.why: The hard sessions are back to back, at the weekend.

options.text: Sat intervals, Sun tempo, Mon easy, Tue easy, Wed easy
options.why: Hard sessions back to back again, just in a different place.

variants.stem: How strong is the evidence that a time-crunched amateur does just as well with a zone 2-heavy plan as with a polarised one?

options.text: Weak: a few small, short trials, mostly in runners
options.why: Right: 30–42 people, 8–10 weeks, all runners.

options.text: Strong: several RCTs agree
options.why: They broadly agree, but they are small and short, so the grade drops.

options.text: Disputed: the trials contradict each other
options.why: They mostly agree: all plans improved with small differences.

options.text: Moderate: the meta-analyses settled it
options.why: The meta-analyses mainly include trained athletes and don't settle the amateur question.
